summary.title: From SmPC to pack
points: Printed packs start as approved text: SmPC, labelling and PIL, following the QRD template.
Text is regulatory; artwork is the design that shows it exactly.
Any wording that differs from the approved text is a compliance problem.
In a DCP, English texts are agreed by Day 210; translations follow in the national phase.
Draft artwork during clock-stops; finalise once translations are approved.

exercises.scenario: A carton says 'take with food'; the approved text says 'take with or without food'.

questions.prompt: What is this?
options: A design choice that's acceptable if the meaning is clear to patients
A compliance error: artwork must match the approved text

questions.prompt: Which template sets the standard headings?
options: The CTD Module 3 template from the dossier owner

exercises.scenario: The DCP is in its Day 105 clock-stop.

questions.prompt: What can the artwork team usefully do now?
options: Print final cartons for all countries before the texts are agreed
questions.explanation: So they're ready when texts are final.

questions.prompt: When can a country's artwork be finalised?
options: Before the English texts are agreed
After its translated texts are approved
At Day 0, using the texts submitted with the application

summary.title: Mock-ups and specimens
points: Applications include mock-ups: flat, full-colour layouts of outer and immediate packs.
Some agencies later ask for specimens: real printed samples.
Mock-ups show faces, fonts, colours, Blue Box, Braille and code area, within the die-line.
Label or leaflet changes not linked to the SmPC can use an Art. 61(3) notification: 90 days without objection.
SmPC changes need a variation. Plan mock-ups with translations, not after the licence.

exercises.scenario: Marketing wants to move the logo on the carton. The texts don't change.

questions.prompt: Which route is typical?
options: A Type II variation with a full assessment of the new layout

questions.prompt: When can the change be made?
options: Immediately, as long as the agency is informed afterwards

exercises.scenario: A country asks for 'specimens' after approval.

questions.prompt: What do they want?
options: Actual printed samples of the pack
Flat colour layouts of every face, as submitted with the application

questions.prompt: What frames the flat carton on a mock-up?
options: The FMD code area marked by the serialisation provider
The die-line from the packaging site

summary.title: Blue Box and Braille
points: The Blue Box holds each country's required particulars: legal status, codes, reimbursement.
The CMDh publishes each country's list; differences force country-specific packs.
The product name must be in Braille on the carton; strength recommended where several exist.
Braille is embossed during printing, so it's in the artwork and checked on the proof.
Collect Blue Box requirements before artwork starts; a missed item means a reprint.

exercises.scenario: You're starting artwork for four DCP countries.

questions.prompt: What should you collect first?
options: The Braille translation of the whole leaflet for every country
questions.explanation: A missed particular means a reprint.

questions.prompt: Your product comes in 10 and 20 mg. What should the Braille show?
options: The name only, since strength is never recommended
questions.explanation: Strength is recommended where several exist.

exercises.scenario: Proofs come back without Braille.

questions.prompt: Why is that serious?
options: It isn't: Braille can be added by the pharmacy later
It only matters for the leaflet
Braille is embossed at printing, so it must be in the artwork now

questions.prompt: Why does the Blue Box make multi-country packs harder?
options: It replaces the patient leaflet for national information
Each country can require different particulars
It must be printed in blue ink

summary.title: Readability testing
points: The leaflet must reflect consultation with patients: readability (user) testing.
Common standard: 90% find each key point, and 90% of those understand it.
Failed items are rewritten and retested.
Generics can often bridge to the reference product's tested leaflet, with a justification.
A full test takes weeks: check early whether bridging is acceptable.

exercises.scenario: Of 20 participants, 18 find the dosing information and 15 of those understand it.

questions.prompt: Does it meet the common standard?
options: Yes: 90% found it, which is the only criterion that counts
No test is needed for dosing

questions.prompt: What happens to that item?

exercises.scenario: Your generic's leaflet is almost identical to the reference's.

questions.prompt: What can you usually do?
options: Run a full test in every country
Bridge to the reference's tested leaflet, with a justification
Skip testing with no justification at all
Ask the reference holder to test it

questions.prompt: Why check this early?
options: The QP must sign the test

summary.title: Serialisation (FMD)
points: Prescription packs carry a unique identifier (2D DataMatrix) and an anti-tampering device, since February 2019.
Codes are printed at packaging and uploaded to the EU hub, then to national systems.
Pharmacies scan to verify and decommission; mismatches raise alerts.
Before shipping: hub onboarding, product master data per country, coding lines, carton space.
Onboarding and data upload take weeks: start early and confirm data reach each country.

exercises.scenario: Packs are made and released, but product data were never uploaded.

questions.prompt: What happens at the pharmacy?
options: Nothing; the pharmacy enters the code manually and dispenses
Scanning fails or alerts, so the pack can't be dispensed properly
The pack is accepted, as it's released
questions.explanation: Perfectly made packs can still be blocked.

questions.prompt: What does the unique identifier contain?
options: Product code, serial number, batch, expiry, and national number where required

exercises.scenario: A colleague plans hub onboarding for launch week.

questions.prompt: What's wrong?
options: Onboarding and data upload take weeks
Onboarding is only needed after the first sale

questions.prompt: What happens when the pharmacy scans a genuine pack?
options: It's verified and marked as dispensed
It's sent back to the MAH

summary.title: Multilingual packs
points: A pack can carry several languages if every language gives the same particulars.
Pros: fewer SKUs, bigger runs, stock that moves between countries.
Cons: carton space, different Blue Boxes and codes, every wording must fit.
Check: carton size, every country accepts, Blue Boxes coexist, serialisation data reach each system.
Decide early: it changes artwork count, runs and stock planning.

exercises.scenario: You're launching in three small Baltic markets.

questions.prompt: What's the main appeal of a multilingual pack?
options: Fewer SKUs and stock that can move between countries
No Blue Box is needed when several languages share a pack
questions.explanation: Common for groups of smaller markets.

questions.prompt: What's the main constraint?
options: Carton space for all languages, Blue Boxes and codes

exercises.scenario: The multilingual decision is taken after artwork has started.

questions.prompt: What's affected?
options: Artwork count, packaging runs and stock planning

questions.prompt: Which check is about the FMD?
options: Carton size and the space for every language
Serialisation data reaching each national system
questions.explanation: Codes must work in every country.

summary.title: The artwork workflow
points: Each country's artwork follows the same loop; delays come from late texts and correction rounds.
Owner: artwork coordinator; RA approves text, QA for GMP, marketing the design.
Inputs: approved translations, die-line, Blue Box, serialisation area, Braille.
Proofreading word by word, plus Braille, codes and colours, is a GMP control.
Start drafts in clock-stops; one text source; one plan line per country.

exercises.scenario: The artwork used an old die-line from another packaging line.

questions.prompt: What's the risk?
options: The carton won't fit the line and must be reprinted
None, as long as the text matches the approved version

questions.prompt: Who approves the texts on the artwork?
questions.explanation: QA approves for GMP, marketing the design.

exercises.scenario: A recall is traced to a carton misprint.

questions.prompt: Which control should have caught it?
options: The QP's check of the CoA and the batch records

questions.prompt: What most often delays artwork?
options: Waiting for the FMD hub to issue serial numbers
Design work on fonts and colours
Late text approvals and correction rounds

summary.title: Version control after variations
points: When approved texts change, artwork changes too, with a new version per country.
Track: text version, artwork version, implementation deadline, old-stock rules.
Safety changes are usually implemented faster.
Rules vary by country and type of change.
Before every print order, ask RA if any text change is pending.

exercises.scenario: A safety variation is approved two weeks before launch.

questions.prompt: What do you check first?
options: Whether printed packs still match, and the implementation deadline
Whether the BE study needs repeating for the new safety text
Whether the FTO is still valid
questions.explanation: Freshly printed cartons may be obsolete.

questions.prompt: Why can safety changes hurt more?
options: They apply only to new packs after renewal
They can be ignored for generics

exercises.scenario: You're about to order 100,000 cartons for Germany.

questions.prompt: What do you ask RA?
options: Is the QP available to sign the proofs before printing?
questions.explanation: Printing before a text change wastes material.

questions.prompt: What links an artwork version to the licence?
options: The approved text version it comes from
The batch number of the first stock packed with it

summary.title: Texts, mock-ups and the leaflet
points: Artwork shows approved text exactly; differences are compliance errors.
DCP texts are agreed by Day 210; translations in the national phase; drafts during clock-stops.
Mock-ups go with the application; 61(3) for non-SmPC label changes; variations for SmPC changes.
Blue Box per country and Braille name (and strength) on every carton.
Readability: 90/90 standard, or bridge to a tested leaflet.

exercises.scenario: The DCP closes in a month for four countries.

questions.prompt: What should be ready already?
options: Printed cartons for all four countries, ready to pack
Artwork drafts, Blue Box requirements and the bridging justification

questions.prompt: When can each country's artwork be finalised?
options: At Day 210, when the English texts are agreed

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between text and artwork, and why it matters.
questions.modelAnswer: Text (SmPC, labelling, PIL) is regulatory and approved in the procedure; artwork is the design showing it. Any difference on the pack is a compliance error, and changing text needs a variation or notification.

exercises.scenario: After launch, marketing wants a new carton layout, and RA updates a side-effect in the SmPC.

questions.prompt: Which routes apply?
options: 61(3) for the layout; a variation for the SmPC change
61(3) for both, since neither changes the licence
questions.explanation: Linked to the SmPC or not.

questions.prompt: Which carton element can't be added after printing?

summary.title: Codes, languages and the workflow
points: FMD: unique identifier and tamper seal; hub onboarding and data before first shipment.
Multilingual packs cut SKUs but strain space, Blue Boxes and codes.
Artwork loop per country: texts, die-line, Blue Box, code area, Braille, proofreading.
Proofreading is a GMP control; misprints lead to recalls.
Version control links artwork to text; check for pending changes before printing.

exercises.scenario: Two months before launch, you review artwork status for five countries.

questions.prompt: What does the plan show for each?
options: Text approval, proof rounds and printer slot
Only the country's launch date, since artwork follows automatically

questions.prompt: Which FMD item must be done before packs ship?
options: Hub onboarding and product data per country

questions.prompt: List three checks before choosing a multilingual pack.
questions.modelAnswer: That the carton is big enough; that every country accepts it; that the Blue Box items can coexist (and that serialisation data reach every national system).

exercises.scenario: Cartons were printed last week; RA now says a text variation is approved.

questions.prompt: What do you check?
options: Implementation deadline and old-stock rules per country
Nothing; printed cartons can always be used until expiry
questions.explanation: Rules vary by country and change type.

questions.prompt: What habit would have prevented this?
options: Printing earlier, before any variation could be approved
Asking RA about pending text changes before printing

summary.title: Artworks: the whole picture
points: Approved texts (QRD) drive artwork; any mismatch is a compliance error.
Mock-ups go to agencies; 61(3) or variations handle later changes.
Each country needs its Blue Box; Braille is embossed at printing.
Readability: 90/90 or bridging.
FMD codes need hub onboarding and data before shipping.
Artwork is often on the critical path: proofread, version-control, check pending changes.

exercises.scenario: You plan artwork for a DCP in five countries, two of them small markets sharing a pack.

questions.prompt: When should drafts start?
options: After the national licences are granted in every country
questions.explanation: So they're ready when texts are final.

questions.prompt: How many artwork lines do you track?
options: Five, even for the shared pack
Four: three single-country packs and one shared pack

questions.prompt: Which inputs do you need for each artwork?
options: Approved translations, die-line, Blue Box, code area, Braille

exercises.scenario: One week before launch: packs are printed and released, but a pharmacy test scan fails.

questions.prompt: What's the likely cause?
options: A Braille error on the carton made during embossing
Product master data not uploaded or not reaching the national system

questions.prompt: What else should you confirm before shipping?
options: No pending text change makes the print obsolete
That the RMS has confirmed the national licence numbers

questions.prompt: In two sentences, explain why artwork is so often on the critical path in the last months.
questions.modelAnswer: Country artwork can only be finalised after translated texts are approved, then it needs proof rounds and a printer slot before packaging can run. Late texts, correction rounds and pending text changes all push the printed packs, and so the launch.
